strengths: The paper presents a useful post-processing approach to Gaussian-splatting error estimation: project training residuals and visibility onto primitives, render these representations into novel views, and learn a pixel-wise error predictor. This integrates naturally with the existing renderer and does not require modifying reconstruction training.

The improvements extend beyond comparison with unmodified FisherRF. Against FisherRF features using the same regression framework, Table 1 improves multi-view depth AUSE from 0.127 to 0.099 on LF and from 0.226 to 0.132 on TUM using direction-independent features. This supports the value of the proposed representations.

Foreground results are particularly strong. In Table 3, multi-view depth correlations reach 0.859/0.849 on LF/TUM versus 0.757/0.700 for regression-FisherRF; rendering-error correlations reach 0.842/0.851 versus 0.751/0.766. These are meaningful improvements for object-focused reconstruction assessment.

The experimental analysis covers 15 scenes, RGB and depth errors, foreground and full-scene evaluation, feature selection, directional features, regression choices, and cross-scene transfer. Table 4 provides encouraging evidence of transferable foreground predictors: multi-scene TUM training achieves depth correlations of 0.688 on LF and 0.645 on TUM.
weaknesses: The correctness of the principal baseline is insufficiently established. Appendix A identifies diagonal Fisher-information entries as parameter variances, whereas covariance approximations normally involve inverse, typically regularized, information. The manuscript does not clarify the inversion or regularization actually implemented. Together with the consistently negative full-scene rendering-error correlations for standard FisherRF, this warrants verification. It does not prove an implementation error, but it materially weakens confidence in the headline comparison. The regression-enhanced baseline is a valuable partial mitigation.

The state-of-the-art claim exceeds the comparisons provided. FisherRF and its proposed modification are the only evaluated competing approaches, despite the discussion of other directly relevant Gaussian-splatting uncertainty methods, including references [1] and [6]. Different training requirements should be acknowledged, but comparison with at least another uncertainty approach would help establish whether the contribution advances beyond one baseline family.

The evidence establishes error association and some ranking quality, rather than reliable error magnitudes or calibrated uncertainty. Pearson correlation is insensitive to bias and scale; the manuscript explicitly avoids absolute regression evaluation because of distribution shifts. AUSE is reported only for in-scene, full-scene depth estimation. Consequently, the stronger reliability motivations and the usefulness of transferred RGB-error estimates remain less well supported than the foreground correlation results.

Reproducibility and evaluation independence are under-specified. The paper omits key gradient-boosting hyperparameters, exact reconstruction and regression view splits, multi-scene training composition and exclusion rules, and the procedure for fitting directional representations into spherical harmonics. Feature subsets are selected using held-out-view performance and subsequently evaluated on all scenes, without a clearly independent selection/test protocol. The code link is a placeholder, and preprocessing time, inference cost, and memory overhead are unreported.

Generalization is substantially more conditional than the broad claims suggest. In Table 4, the LF-trained, multi-scene directional model has full-scene depth correlations of -0.030 on LF and -0.004 on TUM, despite strong foreground performance. Moreover, transfer removes the need for target-scene holdout labels, but constructing the target-scene features still requires training-view visibility and residual information; the statement that target-scene GS training data are unnecessary needs this qualification. Overall, the substantial foreground gains and practical formulation balance against unresolved baseline validity and evaluation-protocol concerns, placing the submission near the acceptance boundary.

strengths: The method offers a useful post-processing approach: project training residuals and visibility statistics onto Gaussian primitives, render these features into novel views, and learn pixel-wise error predictors without modifying GS training. The representation is interpretable and applicable to both depth and RGB error prediction.

The reported improvements extend beyond an unsupervised baseline. Against FisherRF features processed by the same regression approach, single-view foreground depth correlations improve from 0.698 to 0.835 on LF and from 0.521 to 0.745 on TUM (Table 3). Full-scene depth AUSE also improves from 0.133 to 0.112 on LF and from 0.328 to 0.213 on TUM (Table 1). These are meaningful empirical merits.

The experiments examine 15 scenes, foreground and background regions, two prediction targets, different supervision amounts, feature selection, directional features, and spatial context. The supplementary per-scene results expose substantial performance variation rather than reporting aggregate results alone.

Cross-scene foreground prediction provides promising evidence of transferable information. With multi-scene TUM training, directional features achieve average depth correlations of 0.688 on LF and 0.645 on TUM (Table 4).
weaknesses: The sole external baseline has an unresolved technical ambiguity. Appendix A identifies diagonal Fisher information entries with parameter variances, whereas covariance is ordinarily approximated using the inverse of a regularized information matrix. The manuscript does not specify inversion or regularization sufficiently to establish whether this is merely incorrect exposition or an implementation issue. FisherRF's uniformly negative full-scene RGB-error correlations make this clarification particularly consequential. The regression-FisherRF comparison is valuable, but does not resolve whether its underlying features were correctly constructed. Other cited GS uncertainty methods, including [1], are not evaluated, so the state-of-the-art claim is insufficiently established.

Reproducibility is materially incomplete. The paper does not adequately specify GS training settings and image splits, gradient-boosting implementation and hyperparameters, exact multi-view/multi-scene training partitions, or the procedure for fitting directional functions to spherical harmonics. The code link is only github.com/TBA. In particular, the cross-scene protocol needs explicit training and test scene membership to make its central generalization claim independently verifiable.

The strongest generalization claims exceed the evidence for complete scenes. In Table 4, multi-scene LF training with directional features produces full-scene depth correlations of -0.030 on LF and -0.004 on TUM; Appendix C also acknowledges failure to generalize to the sole outdoor scene, torch. Foreground transfer is substantially stronger, but relies on object separation and separately trained regressors. Furthermore, the claim of operating without access to a new scene's GS training data conflicts with constructing that scene's residual and visibility features unless those representations were precomputed and retained. Avoiding new holdout labels is a narrower, defensible claim.

The evaluation primarily establishes association with error, not accuracy of predicted error magnitudes or calibrated uncertainty. Pearson correlation is insensitive to scale and offset, and the paper explicitly avoids regression accuracy metrics because of distribution shifts. AUSE helps substantiate error ranking, but is reported only for in-scene full-image depth prediction. Consequently, the evidence for transferable RGB uncertainty and reliability-sensitive applications is considerably weaker than the framing suggests.

The feature study does not cleanly isolate the contribution of training residuals versus visibility and coverage. Backward selection is driven by depth-error correlation, where residual features rank poorly, without corresponding controlled visibility-only and error-only comparisons for both targets. Moreover, selection uses held-out-view performance and selected subsets are subsequently evaluated on all scenes without a clearly independent selection/test partition. This limits the evidential value of the compact-feature results, although it does not invalidate the full-feature comparisons.

The promising foreground gains support a worthwhile contribution, but uncertainty about the baseline construction and insufficient specification of the evaluation protocol prevent a confident acceptance recommendation. These concerns, together with the gap between demonstrated error correlation and the broader claims, determine the weak-reject assessment; limited benchmark breadth or presentation errors alone would not.

strengths: The paper proposes a useful post-processing approach: project training residuals and visibility onto Gaussian primitives, render these features into novel views, and learn pixel-wise error predictors. The construction is interpretable and does not require changing Gaussian Splatting optimization.

The strongest results show substantial improvements over a supervision-matched baseline. In Table 3, single-view foreground depth correlations improve from regression-FisherRF's 0.698/0.521 to 0.835/0.745 on LF/TUM; rendering-error correlations improve from 0.704/0.645 to 0.822/0.756.

The improvements extend beyond Pearson correlation. Table 1 reports single-view full-scene depth AUSE of 0.112/0.213 versus regression-FisherRF's 0.133/0.328 on LF/TUM. This supports the usefulness of the proposed features for ranking unreliable pixels.

The experiments cover 15 scenes, RGB and depth errors, foreground/background evaluation, directional features, regression alternatives, feature selection, and cross-scene transfer. The supplementary per-scene results expose variability rather than reporting only favorable averages.

Cross-scene foreground prediction is promising: the TUM-trained multi-scene directional model reaches mean correlations of 0.667 for depth and 0.577 for rendering error across the two datasets in Table 4.
weaknesses: The FisherRF baseline requires technical clarification. Appendix A identifies diagonal Fisher-information entries as parameter variances, whereas a variance approximation ordinarily involves inverse information with appropriate regularization. The manuscript does not establish whether this is merely inaccurate wording or an implementation issue. Given the negative full-scene correlations and reliance on FisherRF as the sole baseline family, this uncertainty materially affects the comparative evidence.

Reproducibility is insufficiently specified: gradient-boosting implementation and hyperparameters, precise GS/regression/test view splits, multi-scene training membership, and spherical-harmonic fitting details are missing or unclear. The code URL is a placeholder. In particular, the cross-scene tables do not make exclusion of each evaluated scene from multi-scene regressor training sufficiently auditable.

The evidence supports error ranking more strongly than calibrated error estimation. Pearson correlation is insensitive to offset and positive rescaling, and normalized AUSE assesses ordering. No error-magnitude accuracy or calibration results establish that predicted values can support the reliability decisions motivating the work.

Generalization is substantially narrower than the broad claims suggest. All scenes are object-centric; full-scene rendering correlations remain modest, and the LF-trained multi-scene directional model has mean full-scene depth correlation of -0.017 in Table 4. Moreover, transfer removes the need for target-scene regression holdouts, but constructing the proposed features still requires target-scene training views and residuals, contrary to the statement about needing no access to GS training data.

The state-of-the-art claim is not established against other relevant GS uncertainty approaches discussed in the paper, particularly reference [1]. Feature selection also uses holdout performance to choose subsets subsequently evaluated on overlapping scenes/views, limiting independent support for the compact-feature claims. Overall, the substantial foreground gains make this a credible contribution, but baseline ambiguity and incomplete experimental specification keep the recommendation at the acceptance boundary.

strengths: PRIMU provides a useful, interpretable post-hoc approach: training-view residuals and visibility statistics are attached to Gaussian primitives, rendered into novel views, and combined through regression. This preserves the underlying reconstruction and offers a practical contribution beyond stochastic or Fisher-based uncertainty estimates.

The quantitative gains are substantial across several datasets. In Table 1, direction-dependent PRIMU achieves rendering-error AUSE of 0.286/0.378/0.281 on LF/MipNeRF360/LLFF, outperforming all reported baselines. On LF depth estimation, PRIMU achieves 0.115 AUSE and 0.722 Pearson correlation, versus 0.173 and 0.243 for BayesRays.

The regression-based FisherRF comparison meaningfully controls for the benefit of supervised regression. Under matching one-view gradient-boosting setups in Table 3, PRIMU improves foreground depth correlation from 0.698 to 0.835 on LF and from 0.521 to 0.745 on TUM. This supports the value of the proposed features themselves.

The experimental analysis covers direction dependence, feature selection, foreground/background separation, regressor choice, and cross-scene transfer. The holdout-free active-view-selection application also demonstrates practical utility: Table 6 improves PSNR from FisherRF's 20.392 to 20.721 while improving SSIM and LPIPS. Together, these supported contributions favor acceptance despite the reservations below.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons in Tables 1–2 mix supervision regimes: PRIMU receives held-out error labels, including ground-truth depth for depth regression, whereas the original uncertainty baselines do not. The matched regression-based FisherRF experiment partly addresses this, but only in the separate LF/TUM study. Thus, the headline gains cannot be attributed entirely to the primitive representations.

Cross-scene transfer is substantially less reliable than within-scene prediction. In Table 8, LF-trained multi-scene PRIMU reaches only 0.039 whole-view depth correlation on unseen LF scenes; the directional variant reaches -0.030, compared with within-scene correlations above 0.7. Foreground transfer is considerably stronger. The appendix acknowledges scale issues, but the evidence supports conditional transfer rather than broadly reliable operation without target-scene holdout data.

The evaluation establishes error ranking and correlation, not calibrated error magnitudes or probabilistic uncertainty. AUSE and Pearson correlation can remain favorable despite substantial prediction-scale errors. The statement that R² is inapplicable because input and target ranges shift is not convincing; those shifts are precisely a relevant generalization challenge. This limits the interpretation of predicted errors for safety-related decisions.

Reproducibility and efficiency are insufficiently documented. The manuscript does not specify the gradient-boosting implementation and hyperparameters, exact UE view splits and multi-view counts, or how the directional functions are fitted to spherical harmonics. Runtime and memory measurements are also absent, leaving the practical cost of constructing and rendering the feature representations unclear.

The active-view-selection evidence is promising but incomplete: Table 6 reports one aggregate 20-view endpoint without random or continued farthest-point selection, per-scene results, or variability across runs. This makes the robustness and practical significance of the 0.329 dB gain over FisherRF difficult to assess.

Several presentation claims overstate the tables. Section 4 claims that all one-view foreground settings achieve AUSE below 0.1 and correlation above 0.8, whereas TUM PRIMU reports rendering/depth correlations of 0.756/0.745. Gradient boosting also does not uniformly outperform linear regression on entire TUM views. These are correctable reporting problems rather than failures of the central method.

strengths: PRIMU provides a useful, interpretable contribution: training-view errors and visibility statistics are projected onto Gaussian primitives, rendered into novel-view features, and combined through supervised regression. The construction is compatible with an existing reconstruction and does not require retraining the Gaussian scene.

The reported error-ranking improvements are substantial across several datasets. In Table 1, PRIMU* reduces rendering-error AUSE to 0.286 on LF, 0.378 on MipNeRF360, and 0.281 on LLFF, outperforming all listed baselines. Table 2 also shows strong depth-error prediction, with Pearson correlation of 0.728.

Table 3 provides an important control for the benefit of supervised regression by applying the same regression approach to six FisherRF-derived features. PRIMU retains meaningful advantages: with one holdout view, object-centric TUM depth correlation improves from 0.521 to 0.745, and rendering correlation from 0.645 to 0.756. This supports the utility of the proposed features beyond simply adding a regressor.

The experiments investigate feature redundancy, directional encoding, foreground/background differences, regression choices, and transfer to unseen scenes. The active-view-selection application also provides evidence of practical value without requiring holdout supervision: Table 6 improves PSNR from FisherRF's 20.392 to 20.721 while improving SSIM and LPIPS.

Overall, the consistent empirical gains and controlled feature comparison support weak acceptance. The contribution is primarily an effective empirical representation and prediction pipeline; its value does not depend on introducing a new probabilistic uncertainty formulation.
weaknesses: The headline comparisons in Tables 1–2 use unequal supervision: PRIMU learns from a labeled holdout view, including ground-truth depth for depth-error prediction, whereas the original baselines do not receive equivalent error supervision. The regression-based FisherRF comparison partly addresses this, but only in the separate scene-separation setup. Consequently, the headline gains cannot be attributed entirely to the primitive representation.

The evidence establishes error ranking and correlation, rather than calibrated uncertainty or accurate absolute error prediction. Both AUSE and Pearson correlation can remain favorable under substantial miscalibration. The statement that R² is inapplicable because input and target ranges shift is not technically justified; such shifts can instead expose prediction failures. This limits the safety-critical interpretation of the results.

Cross-scene generalization is conditional and considerably weaker than within-scene performance. In Table 8, multi-scene LF-trained PRIMU* has whole-scene LF depth correlation of -0.03, despite object-centric correlation of 0.663. Whole-scene rendering correlations also remain modest. Appendix C acknowledges limitations, but the abstract's generalization claim needs this qualification.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the manuscript does not specify the main gradient-boosting hyperparameters, exact holdout selection and multi-view counts, or the fitting procedure used to encode directional representations in spherical harmonics. Runtime and memory measurements are also absent, leaving the practical cost of constructing and rendering the feature bank unclear.

The active-view-selection evidence is promising but limited to one final view budget and dataset-level averages. There are no random or continued farthest-point selection controls, per-scene results, or variation across runs. These omissions particularly limit confidence in the modest PSNR advantage and the assertion that it is achieved reliably.

Some technical descriptions and result summaries need correction. Appendix A describes Fisher-information diagonal entries as parameter variances, whereas covariance approximations normally involve inverse information; the implementation cannot be verified from this description. The claim that all one-view object-centric settings achieve correlation above 0.8 also contradicts Table 3's TUM results. These are specific accuracy concerns, although they do not by themselves invalidate the reported PRIMU improvements.

strengths: PRIMU provides a useful, interpretable post-hoc approach to Gaussian-splatting error prediction. Projecting training residuals and coverage statistics onto primitives, rendering them into novel views, and combining them with lightweight regression is a coherent contribution that preserves the underlying reconstruction.

The reported improvements are substantial across several datasets. In Table 1, direction-dependent PRIMU achieves rendering-error AUSE of 0.286/0.378/0.281 on LF/MipNeRF360/LLFF, outperforming the evaluated baselines. For LF depth estimation, PRIMU achieves AUSE 0.115 and Pearson correlation 0.722, versus 0.173 and 0.243 for BayesRays.

The regression-based FisherRF comparison helps separate feature quality from the benefit of supervised regression. With the same one-view gradient-boosting setup, Table 3 reports foreground depth correlations of 0.835/0.745 for PRIMU on LF/TUM versus 0.698/0.521 for regression-based FisherRF. This supports the utility of the proposed primitive representations.

The experiments extend beyond headline comparisons to feature selection, directional dependence, foreground/background separation, cross-scene transfer, and spatial context. Active view selection also demonstrates practical utility without requiring holdout supervision: Table 6 improves PSNR from FisherRF's 20.392 to 20.721 while improving SSIM and LPIPS. Together, these results favor acceptance despite the limitations below.
weaknesses: The main comparisons in Tables 1–2 mix supervision regimes: PRIMU receives ground-truth error targets from a held-out view, including depth ground truth for depth prediction, whereas the original baselines do not receive equivalent regression supervision. Table 3 meaningfully addresses this for FisherRF, but only in the scene-separation setting. The main benchmark gains therefore cannot be attributed entirely to the proposed features.

The evidence establishes error ranking and correlation, rather than calibrated uncertainty or accurate absolute error prediction. Both reported metrics tolerate some substantial miscalibration. The statement that R² is inapplicable because input and target ranges shift is not justified; such shifts can expose meaningful prediction failures. This limits the safety-critical reliability implications, although it does not invalidate the error-ranking contribution.

Cross-scene generalization is conditional. In Table 8, PRIMU trained across LF scenes achieves only 0.039 correlation for full-view LF depth error, and the direction-dependent variant reaches -0.030, despite much stronger foreground results. The appendix acknowledges scale-related difficulties, but the evidence does not establish generally reliable deployment without scene-specific holdout data.

Reproducibility and efficiency are insufficiently documented. The manuscript specifies feature thresholds, concentration, and harmonic degree, but does not adequately specify gradient-boosting hyperparameters, exact UE view splits and holdout selection, or the numerical procedure for encoding directional features into spherical harmonics. No timing or memory measurements substantiate the practical cost of constructing and rendering the feature representations.

Some claims exceed the reported evidence. Section 4 states that all one-view object-centric configurations achieve AUSE below 0.1 and correlations above 0.8, whereas Table 3 includes TUM correlations of 0.756 and 0.745 for direction-independent PRIMU. Directional features also sometimes reduce performance. For active view selection, aggregate results lack variability estimates and random or geometric selection baselines, leaving the robustness and incremental value of the modest PSNR gain uncertain.
